## Magnitude and direction {#iv1-meaning .vector-lesson}

::: {.split}
<div class="column-block">
<h3>Scalar quantities</h3>
<p>A number, with units where appropriate.</p>
<ul><li>Distance</li><li>Speed</li><li>Time and temperature</li></ul>
</div>
<div class="column-block">
<h3>Vector quantities</h3>
<p>Both magnitude and direction.</p>
<ul><li>Displacement</li><li>Velocity</li><li>Acceleration and force</li></ul>
</div>
:::

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
A scalar can be positive, negative or zero. Its sign alone does not make it a vector.
:::

<div class="booklet-cue">Booklet §1.1 · p. 1</div>

::: notes
Ask students to explain distance versus displacement, and speed versus velocity. Temperature below zero is a counterexample to the old slide's claim that scalar quantities are only positive. Distinguish a scalar quantity from a real number acting as a multiplier, which appears later. Signed 1D displacement records direction relative to the selected positive axis. Different physical quantities must not be added merely because each is a vector.
:::
